title: Our Crooked Compass
author: Lee LeFever
summary: Lee LeFever, writing on the science of explanation, examines reason as both a personal way of thinking and a social act of communication. He adopts Mercier and Sperber's hypothesis that reasoning evolved to devise and evaluate arguments meant to persuade. Using the example of a spouse asking why you grabbed an umbrella, he shows the two sides: private logic and the shared reasoning others can test. Personal reasoning is unreliable because it rests on flawed prior knowledge and is bent by motivated reasoning. Communicating it requires representing it in speech, writing or drawing, a treacherous jump between minds that is why explanation works best as a conversation. Reason also has a dark side, since people can make almost anything sound reasonable. He closes with three questions for inspecting your own reasoning and advice to share reasons openly.
points: LeFever treats reason as a test of evidence that works at both a personal and a social level, and says explanation lives where they meet.
Following Mercier and Sperber, he holds that the function of reasoning is argumentative, to devise and evaluate persuasive arguments.
Personal reasoning is flawed because it rests on existing knowledge that may be wrong and is shaped by motivated reasoning.
The jump from mind to a shared representation is treacherous, so explanation is best handled as a conversation that adjusts as it goes.
He offers three questions for checking your own reasoning and urges explainers to share their reasons so audiences can test them.
quotes: Reason is a guide for what can or should be believed. Put another way, it’s a test of evidence.
Our hypothesis is that the function of reasoning is argumentative. It is to devise and evaluate arguments intended to persuade.
This interaction between personal and social reasoning is at the heart of explanation.
When we use personal reasoning to come to a conclusion, it doesn’t make the conclusion correct. Our reasoning is often flawed and based on existing knowledge that may or may not be accurate.
A clear, sound argument gives someone a path to follow, but it doesn’t guarantee they’ll see what you see, or come to the same conclusion.
Some people can make almost anything sound reasonable, and when we need answers, their reasoning can be seductive.
Your audience will reason about your message with the same biases. Share your reasons openly, so they can test them against their own thinking.
